steps.say: Angular is a framework from Google for building web apps, written in TypeScript.
You build the screen from components: small pieces made of a class, a template and styles.
Angular gives you routing, forms, HTTP and testing tools in one place, so you do not choose each one yourself.
When your data changes, Angular updates only the parts of the page that need it.
The browser runs the finished app and the user sees a fast, interactive page.
TypeScript is JavaScript with types. You say what kind of value a variable, input or function holds.
The compiler and your editor check those types while you type.
If you pass a number where text is expected, you see the error at once, not later in the browser.
Interfaces, classes and decorators are the parts of TypeScript you will use most in Angular.
When everything checks out, TypeScript is turned into plain JavaScript for the browser.
Install Node.js first. Angular tools run on it.
Node comes with npm, the package manager that downloads tools and libraries.
Use npm to install the Angular CLI, which gives you the ng command.
Run ng version to confirm that it is installed.
Now ng can create, run and build projects for you.
Start with the basics: your first app, components and templates.
Next you manage state with signals and services, and collect input with forms.
Then connect real data: routing between pages and HTTP calls to an API.
Advanced topics follow: RxJS, change detection, server-side rendering, testing and security.
Projects tie it together, and the last lessons show how to deploy.

Create Your First Angular App with the C.title: From ng new to the browser

steps.say: Run ng new and answer the questions. The CLI creates a complete project.
Move into the folder and run ng serve to start the development server.
Open localhost:4200 in the browser and your first app appears.
Change a file and save it. The browser reloads by itself.

Angular Project Structure Explained.title: Where things live in a project

steps.say: main.ts is the entry point. It starts the app.
It passes in app.config.ts, where you list app-wide settings and services.
It then loads the root component, which holds the page layout.
app.routes.ts says which component shows for each URL.
The result is drawn inside index.html, the single page the browser loads.
A component is a class with a decorator that tells Angular how to use it.
Its template is HTML that shows the data from the class.
Its styles apply only to this component.
The selector gives it a custom tag name.
Put that tag in another template, and Angular draws your component there.
The Angular CLI is one tool for the whole life of a project.
ng new creates a project. You can keep several apps side by side in separate folders.
ng generate makes components, services and more with the right files and names.
ng update upgrades Angular and runs migrations that change your code for you. Upgrade one major version at a time.
ng build creates the optimised files you deploy.
A class property holds a value, for example title.
In the template, double curly braces read that value.
Angular turns it into text on the page.
When the property changes, the text on the page updates.
You can also write small expressions inside the braces, such as a calculation.
Square brackets bind a class value to an element property, like [disabled]="isBusy".
The element always shows the current value. Angular keeps it in sync.
Round brackets listen to events, like (click)="save()".
The event calls your method in the component class.
The method changes the data, and property bindings update the screen.
Two-way binding keeps a property and an input in sync in both directions.
Property to input: the box shows the current value of name.
Input to property: when the user types, name is updated.
Anything else that shows name now shows the new value too.
The banana-in-a-box [(ngModel)] is shorthand for a property binding plus an event binding.
A signal holds a value and tells Angular whenever that value changes.
You read it by calling it like a function: count().
The template now depends on the signal.
Call set or update to change the value.
Angular knows exactly which parts of the page used the signal, and refreshes only those.
Global styles in styles.css apply to every page of the app.
Component styles apply only to that component.
View encapsulation is how Angular keeps a component's styles from leaking out.
Libraries such as Bootstrap and Font Awesome are added once and used through classes.
The browser combines all of them into the final look.
Control flow decides which parts of the template exist at all.
@if shows its block when the condition is true.
@else gives the block for when it is false.
Only the matching block is added to the page. The other is not in the page at all.
@switch picks one block out of many cases, like the status of an order.
You have an array of items, such as products.
@for repeats its block once for each item.
The track expression tells Angular which item is which, usually its id.
The page gets one element per item.
When the array changes, Angular uses the tracking to add, move or remove only what changed.
Older Angular code uses *ngIf, *ngFor and *ngSwitch, which you still meet in many projects.
trackBy was the old way to track list items. @for uses a track expression instead.
Angular provides a migration that converts templates to the new control flow for you.
The result is the same behaviour with the built-in @if, @for and @switch blocks.
Review the changes and run your tests. Your app keeps working.
State in your component decides how an element looks.
A class binding adds or removes a single class when the value is true or false.
ngClass handles several classes at once, from an object or a list.
A style binding sets one CSS property, with a unit if you need it.
The element updates whenever the state changes.
Some values depend on others. A computed signal calculates one from other signals.
total reads price and quantity.
When either changes, total is recalculated. It is also cached until then.
An effect runs code whenever the signals it reads change.
Use effects for things like logging or saving to storage, not to calculate values.
The cart keeps its lines in one signal.
Pressing Add updates the signal with a new line.
The item count is a computed signal that reads the lines.
The total is another computed signal, so it is always correct.
The cart view shows both values and refreshes with no extra code.
A parent often needs to give data to a child component.
In the parent template, bind the value to the child's input with square brackets.
The child declares the input with input() or input.required().
Inside the child, read it by calling product().
Data flows one way, from parent to child. When the parent value changes, the child updates.
A child tells its parent that something happened with an output.
The child emits an event, optionally with a value.
The parent listens with round brackets and runs its own method.
model() combines an input and an output, so the child can change a value the parent owns.
With model(), the parent can use [(value)] for two-way binding with the child.
A pipe changes how a value is shown, without changing the value itself.
Put the raw value in the template and add a pipe after the bar sign.
The date pipe turns a timestamp into readable text in the format you choose.
The currency pipe adds the symbol and decimals. Uppercase and lowercase pipes change text.
Pipes can take options and can be chained one after another.
The async pipe subscribes to an observable or promise and shows its latest value.
It also unsubscribes when the component is destroyed, so you cannot forget to.
The keyvalue pipe lets you loop over the keys and values of an object.
You can also use a pipe in TypeScript, by injecting it or creating it and calling transform.
A component has a life: it is created, it updates, then it is removed.
ngOnInit runs once after the inputs are set. It is the place to load initial data.
ngOnChanges runs when an input value changes. DoCheck runs on every change detection.
ngAfterViewInit runs once the view and child components exist.
ngOnDestroy runs just before removal. Stop timers and subscriptions here.
A template reference variable, like #box, gives a name to an element or component in the template.
viewChild() lets your class get hold of something inside its own template.
contentChild() gets something the parent projected into your component.
ng-container groups elements or holds an @if without adding an extra element to the page.
Once you have the reference, you can call its methods or read its value.
A service is a class that holds logic or data you want to reuse, such as API calls.
Mark it with @Injectable and provide it, often with providedIn: root.
A component asks for it with inject(). It does not create it with new.
Another component asks, and gets the same instance.
This keeps components small and makes services easy to replace in tests.
Two components that are not parent and child still need the same data.
Put the data in a service. It lives as one shared instance.
The service keeps the state in a signal.
Component A calls a service method to change it.
Component B reads the signal and updates by itself.
Angular has a tree of injectors that follows your component tree.
A component asks for a service. Angular looks in its own providers first.
If it is not found, Angular moves up to the parent, and finally to the root.
A provider on a component gives that branch its own instance.
Flags change the search: @Self only here, @SkipSelf starts at the parent, @Optional allows no result.
In a reactive form you build the form model in your class.
It is a FormGroup holding a FormControl for each field.
The template connects to it with [formGroup] and formControlName.
As the user types, the model always has the current values.
On submit, read form.value and send it where it needs to go.
Validators are rules a control must satisfy.
Attach built-in ones such as required, minLength and email.
Angular checks them each time the value changes and sets the status.
Show an error message only when the control is invalid and touched.
A custom validator is a function that returns an error object or null.
In a template-driven form, most of the setup is in the HTML.
Add ngModel and a name to each input. Angular builds the form model for you.
Use HTML attributes like required for validation.
The form tracks values and validity.
The ngSubmit event gives your code the values. It suits small, simple forms.
FormControl is one field. FormGroup groups fields into one form.
FormBuilder is a shorter way to create them.
setValue needs every field. patchValue lets you update only some.
valueChanges is an observable that emits each time a value changes.
statusChanges emits when the form becomes valid or invalid.
Selects, checkboxes and radio buttons work with form controls just like text inputs.
A select or radio group stores one chosen value.
A checkbox stores true or false.
Typed forms know the type of each control, so mistakes show up in your editor.
FormRecord is for groups where the keys are not known in advance.
Custom validators encode your own rules, such as a password policy.
Async validators wait for a result, for example checking if a username is taken. The control shows pending meanwhile.
A cross-field validator sits on the group and compares fields, like password and confirm.
setValidators changes the rules at runtime. Call updateValueAndValidity afterwards.
Routing lets one Angular app show different pages for different URLs, without a full reload.
You list routes in app.routes.ts. Each route pairs a path with a component.
When the URL matches, the router picks that component.
router-outlet marks the spot in the layout where the chosen page is drawn.
Use routerLink instead of plain links, so clicking changes the page without reloading.
Part of a URL can carry data. The router reads it for you.
The route /products/:id matches the URL.
Route parameters are required parts of the path, like the id.
Query parameters come after the question mark and are optional, like sort or page.
The component reads both, and loads the right data.
Use routerLink for links in a template.
Use router.navigate when code decides where to go, for example after saving.
The router updates the URL and shows the matching component.
ActivatedRoute gives that component its params, query params and route data.
Router events tell you when navigation starts and ends, useful for loading bars.
A guard is a function that decides whether a route may open.
The user tries to open a protected URL.
Before showing the page, the router runs the guard.
If the guard returns true, the page opens.
Otherwise it returns a redirect to the login page. Remember: the server must still check permissions.
There are several guard types, each at a different moment.
CanActivateChild protects all the children of a route at once.
CanDeactivate runs before leaving, so you can warn about unsaved changes.
Resolve fetches data before the page shows.
canMatch decides whether a route definition applies at all, for example by role. Preloading can fetch lazy routes in the background.
Without lazy loading, the first download contains the whole app.
With lazy loading, a page is split into its own file.
The user opens a lazy route.
Only then does the router download that file, using loadComponent or loadChildren.
The page appears. The first load stays small and fast.
Keep API calls in a service, not in the component.
Provide HttpClient with provideHttpClient(), then inject it into the service.
Calling get() returns an observable. Nothing is sent until someone subscribes.
The API replies with JSON.
The component subscribes, or uses the async pipe, and shows the data.
Before a request, set a loading flag so the user sees something is happening.
post() sends data to the API as the request body.
On success, turn off loading and update the screen.
On failure, catch the error and show a clear message, instead of a blank screen.
The same service can cover all the actions your API supports.
Use HttpParams for query parameters such as page or search, and set headers when needed.
PUT replaces a whole item. PATCH changes only some fields.
DELETE removes an item by id.
The API processes each request and returns the result.
An observable is a stream of values over time, like clicks or HTTP results.
Operators are small steps you add with pipe().
map changes each value. filter keeps only the ones you want.
Nothing runs until you subscribe.
Unsubscribe when done, or let the async pipe do it for you.
There are helper functions to create observables.
of emits the values you give it, one after another, then completes.
from turns an array, string or promise into a stream.
fromEvent turns browser events, like clicks, into a stream.
Subscribe to receive the values.
These operators decide how many values you let through.
skip ignores the first values.
take stops after a number of values. first and last pick one value. takeUntil and takeWhile stop on a condition.
tap lets you look at values, for logging, without changing them.
The subscriber gets only what is left, and the stream completes.
debounceTime waits until the user stops typing before it passes on a value.
That means one API call instead of one per key press.
scan keeps a running result and emits it for every value, like a live total.
reduce emits only the final result, when the stream completes.
delay and delayWhen shift values later in time.
An error ends an observable unless you handle it.
retry tries the request again a set number of times.
If it still fails, catchError lets you recover instead of crashing.
Return a fallback value, or use throwError to pass a clearer error on.
finalize runs at the end either way, which is a good place to hide a spinner.
A subject is an observable you can also push values into.
Call next() and every current subscriber receives the value.
Both listeners get the same value.
A BehaviorSubject keeps the latest value, so new subscribers get it immediately.
ReplaySubject replays several past values. AsyncSubject gives only the last, on completion.
A test sets up a situation, does something, and checks the result.
TestBed creates the component with the same setup the app uses.
You create it, change its inputs or click a button, then let Angular update.
Use expect to check the text or value you get.
Vitest runs the file and reports passes and failures. For services, mock the HTTP calls.
Accessibility means people with different needs can use your app.
Start with the right HTML elements: real buttons, links, labels and headings.
Add ARIA attributes only where plain HTML cannot say it.
Everything must work with the keyboard, with a visible focus.
Manage focus when the page changes, so screen reader users know where they are.
A production build minifies and optimises your code.
Unused code is removed, which makes bundles smaller.
Lazy loading keeps the first download small.
Optimise images and use track in lists so less work is done.
Check bundle sizes and measure with Lighthouse. The user gets a faster page.
You will build a task manager from small, reusable parts.
The add form sends a new task to the service.
The service keeps all tasks in one signal.
The list renders them with @for.
Buttons toggle or delete tasks, and a computed filter shows all, active or done.
This project is a dashboard with a list, a detail page and an edit form.
A service talks to the API for all employee data.
The table page shows the list with search and sorting.
A reactive form with validators adds or edits an employee.
Routes connect the pages, and a guard can protect the edit screens.
The capstone combines most of what you learned.
Login uses a guard and sends a token with requests.
Courses load from an API, on lazy routes.
A lesson page reads its id from the route.
Progress is kept in signals and saved back to the API.
Run ng build to create the production files.
Upload the dist folder to a host: Netlify, Firebase Hosting, or your own Nginx server.
Because Angular handles routes in the browser, the host must send index.html for unknown paths.
Without this rewrite, refreshing a deep link gives a 404.
The user opens your URL and the app loads.
linkedSignal is a writable signal that is derived from another signal.
When the source changes, it resets to a new default value.
Unlike computed, you can still set it yourself.
effect() reruns when the signals it reads change.
Use effect for side effects, like saving to storage. Avoid it for computing values.
httpResource loads data from an API and exposes it as signals.
It watches a request signal, such as an id.
When the signal changes, it sends a new request.
The result comes back as value, isLoading and error signals.
The template reads these signals and updates itself. resource() works the same way for any async source.
A directive adds behaviour to an existing element, with no template of its own.
Its selector is an attribute, like appHighlight.
Add that attribute to any element.
The host property binds classes, styles and listens to events on that element.
The element now behaves differently, and you can reuse the directive everywhere.
Content projection lets a parent put its own HTML inside a component.
The component marks a spot with ng-content.
The parent writes content between the component tags.
Angular places that content where the slot is.
An ng-template holds markup that is not drawn until something renders it with ngTemplateOutlet.
Sometimes you do not know in advance which component to show, such as in a dialog.
Choose a component class at runtime.
ViewContainerRef creates it and places it in the page.
It appears like any other component.
Host directives let a component apply a directive's behaviour to itself, without extra template code.
Sometimes you need to reach the element itself.
Inject ElementRef to get a handle on it.
Prefer Renderer2 to change it, which keeps the code safe and portable.
@HostBinding sets host properties, and @HostListener listens for host events.
These decorators are the older style. Newer code uses the host metadata, but you will still read them.
Not everything is a class. A token is a name for a value you want to inject, such as a URL.
A provider says which value the token gets.
The injector looks it up when something asks.
Your service injects the token and receives the value.
In tests, provide a different value or a fake class, and your code does not change.
An interceptor sits between HttpClient and the network, and sees every request.
A request goes out through it.
It can clone the request and add an auth token header.
It also sees the response, so it can handle errors in one place, such as sending the user to login on a 401.
A counter in an interceptor can drive one global loading bar. Register interceptors in provideHttpClient.
As an app grows, the folder layout matters more than any single file.
Group code by feature: orders, users and so on, each with its own components and services.
Put app-wide services in core, and reusable components and pipes in shared.
Features should not reach into each other. Share through core or shared.
Pages are routed components that combine the parts.
Settings that differ between development and production go in configuration.
Provide them through app.config.ts, for example with an injection token.
provideAppInitializer runs a function before the app starts, such as loading remote settings.
Once it has finished, the app starts with the config ready.
Remember that anything in a browser app is public, so never put secrets in it.
Errors will happen. The question is what the user sees.
Provide a custom ErrorHandler to catch errors that nobody else caught.
Send details to a logging service so you can fix them.
Show the user a short, friendly message, not a stack trace.
Handle expected HTTP errors close to the request, and let the global handler catch the rest.
Older Angular apps group code into NgModules.
Modules had their own routing, and lazy modules loaded with loadChildren.
New code uses standalone components, which list their own imports.
Angular provides migration schematics that convert modules to standalone step by step.
Your app does the same job with less boilerplate.
Sometimes a built-in input is not enough, for example a star rating.
ControlValueAccessor lets your component act like a form input.
writeValue receives the value from the form, so your control can show it.
When the user picks a star, call onChange to send the value back.
The form now treats it like any other control, with validation too.
A FormArray holds a list of controls, such as several phone numbers.
It lives inside your FormGroup.
push adds a new control when the user clicks Add.
removeAt removes one by its index.
The template loops over the controls with @for, and the rows follow the array.
Signal forms are a newer way to build forms, based on signals.
You start with a signal holding your data as the model.
The form is created from the model, and the validation rules are described next to it.
Each field exposes its state as signals: value, valid and touched.
Inputs bind to the fields, and on submit you read the model. Check the current docs, as this API is still evolving.
As an app grows, shared state needs a clear owner.
A store is a service that keeps the state in a private signal.
Components never change the state directly. They call methods on the store.
The store exposes read-only computed signals as selectors.
Views read the selectors and update automatically.
Real screens depend on several streams at once.
combineLatest emits whenever any of the streams changes, with the latest value of each.
switchMap then starts a request for that value, and cancels the previous one if it is still running.
share or shareReplay lets many subscribers use one request.
concatMap and mergeMap are other ways to flatten, when order or parallel work matters.
Larger apps use routes inside routes.
A layout component has a router-outlet, and child routes appear inside it.
A resolver fetches data before the page opens, so it never shows empty.
Preloading downloads lazy routes in the background after the first load.
View transitions can animate between pages when the browser supports it.
Change detection is how Angular finds out what to update on screen.
Something happens: a click, a timer, a response, or a signal change.
With zone.js, Angular is told after any async task and then checks components.
Signals tell Angular exactly which view depends on what, so less work is needed.
In a zoneless app, Angular does not need zone.js. Signals and events trigger updates, and the DOM is updated.
A normal Angular app sends an almost empty page and builds the content in the browser.
With SSR, the server runs Angular and builds the page first.
It sends full HTML, so people and search engines see content right away.
The browser shows it at once.
Hydration then attaches Angular to the existing HTML so it becomes interactive, without redrawing.
Search engines need each page to say what it is about.
Set a unique title for every route with the Title service.
Use the Meta service for the description and a canonical link.
Server-side rendering puts all of this in the HTML crawlers receive.
Lazy-load images below the fold with correct sizes, to keep pages fast.
Guards, interceptors and routes can be tested without a real server.
Run a guard function with runInInjectionContext and check what it returns.
For interceptors, use HttpTestingController to see the request and send a fake response.
The router testing harness navigates and lets you check which component showed.
Use setInput on the component fixture to test component inputs.
An end-to-end test uses your app the way a user does.
Playwright opens a real browser and loads your running app.
It clicks buttons and types into fields, finding them by role and label.
Then it checks what appears on the screen.
Keep a few tests for the most important journeys, such as sign-up and checkout.
Treat all input as untrusted.
Angular escapes values in templates, which protects you from XSS. Avoid bypassSecurityTrust unless you really must.
Store tokens carefully. HttpOnly cookies are safer than local storage, and cookies need CSRF protection.
Set security headers such as Content-Security-Policy on your server.
Never rely on the browser alone: the server must check every request.
CI/CD runs your checks and deployment for you, every time.
Pushing code starts the workflow.
The workflow installs dependencies, then runs lint and tests.
If they pass, it builds the app.
It then deploys the result. Keep secrets in GitHub secrets, never in the repository.
A refreshed deep link shows 404 because the server does not know Angular routes. Send index.html for unknown paths.
ExpressionChanged means a value changed after Angular had checked it. Move the change earlier or use signals.
EventTarget typing errors happen because the event target is generic. Cast it to the element you expect.
For SSL on localhost, create and trust a local certificate for the dev server.
Read the error message, find the cause, and fix that.
A module loader or bundler turns many source files into files a browser can load.
Early Angular used SystemJS, which loaded modules in the browser.
Webpack then bundled the app at build time, and was the default for years.
Modern Angular builds with esbuild, and the dev server uses Vite, which is much faster.
You still run ng build and ng serve, so the commands stay the same.
The final project brings the whole course together.
Plan the architecture first: features, routes and clear boundaries.
Add state with signals and load data over HTTP, with errors handled.
Test it, and check accessibility and security.
Add SSR and performance work, then let CI/CD ship it.
